newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW - Japan Oct-Dec GDP data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Japan Oct-Dec GDP data.

text.p: The following is a selection of economists and analysts initial reaction to Japan's October-December GDP (gross domestic product) data, which the government said on Thursday rose a real 1.0 percent quarter on quarter, or an annualised 3.9 percent. For calendar 1996, Japan's GDP grew 3.6 percent in real terms.
PETER MORGAN, HSBC JAMES CAPEL JAPAN:

"It's within expectations. It reflects some pre-consumption tax (hike) demand, some effects of the weak yen on exports and the near-ending of inventory adjustment. We're still waiting for April-June (to see if recovery is solid)."

"The number was by no means a surprise." Compared to the previous quarter, consumption was supported by good sales of passenger cars and increased retail sales. This suggests that consumption was the leading item for the GDP growth in the October-December quarter and for the fiscal year.

"We are forecasting a small plus in the final quarter of the fiscal year. So probably the fiscal year figure will be a little higher than 2.5 (percent, the government) projection. All these indicate, the statistics are confirming, that the recovery is continuing a bit more strongly than before. I think this is a very good prelude for 1997 fiscal year."

The biggest impact from the consumption tax rise was on housing starts as consumers rushed to buy housing before the tax goes up in April. "A sudden drop is expected for the next quarter in housing starts," Kiuchi told Reuters Financial Television.
The effect of the consumption tax rise on other consumer items will emerge more in the next quarter.
"Net exports will make a positive contribution to the GDP and that has been shown in the recent improvement in the trade statistics from the international balance of payments.
"Imports are still increasing, but there is a strong increase in exports. That will provide a pleasant surprise in the short term."
KENNETH COURTIS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE BANK GROUP ASIA:
"These numbers show that the economy probably has a little more momentum than most people thought up until now. Companies are investing more, and they aren't completely irrational."

"I think what they're looking at is that the yen is at 120 to the dollar, growth is stronger in the U.S. than most people thought, China is booming, East Asia is moving and Europe is starting to come out of its funk, so exports are going to be strong. Capital investment is going to be strong, so I think we are actually going to get a surprise over the next few months -- the Japanese economy is going to be stronger than most people think."

"As you look ahead, with the government slowing down domestic growth through these higher taxes, my sense is that export growth is going to be even stronger in the rest of this year. That's what is going to drive the economy -- exports and capital investment which is related to exports.
TOSHIFUMI KAWATA, MANAGER, YAMATANE SECURITIES CO LTD
The bond market bullishness was underscored by an EPA official's remark that Japan's growth will slow in early 1997/98.
Looking at details, housing investment was strong at four percent, suggesting last-minute demand before the scheduled consumption tax increase in April.
But such demand will fall in the 1997/98, implying chances that a temporary economic setback predicted by the government may last longer.
